title: Look at what the rule does

turns.text: When someone says a process may produce unequal results by race, my first worry is that it sounds like an accusation. We are trying to help people.

That purpose matters, and it can stay in the conversation. We can still hold two questions apart: did anyone mean to treat someone differently, and how does the rule actually work for the people who must meet it?
In the practice case, families of color are less likely to return a follow-up form by the deadline. What do we actually know from that?
We know there is a pattern worth examining. We do not yet know the cause. So we look at the form, the mailing, the language it is written in and the deadline, along with the limits of the data.
But the form is the same for everyone. Doesn't that make it fair?

Treating everyone the same way is a starting point, not the finish line. A rule can be neutral on paper and still land differently, because people arrive with different access to mail, time, records and language help.
My practical worry is that we end up lowering the standard for some people, and that would not be fair either.

The standard can stay exactly where it is. What changes is the route to meet it, and that route opens for everyone. Accepting an online reply or adding a translated notice applies to every household, not to one group.
And if the numbers are small, or race is missing from a lot of records, how careful do we need to be?

Very careful. Say where each number came from, how old it is and what it cannot tell you. Then talk with the people who use the process, because their account often points to the cause the data only hints at.
What if someone thinks a coworker treated a family unfairly? That feels like a different conversation.

It is. A concern about one person's conduct goes to the person or area responsible for civil rights complaints. A pattern in results is something your team can examine and change, with an owner and a date to look again.

guidance.title: Two questions about one rule
guidance.text: Here is a distinction worth keeping close. Intent is about what someone meant to do. Effect is about how a rule actually works for the people who must meet it. A deadline can be meant to keep processing consistent and still be harder for some households to meet. A difference in results does not tell you the cause. It tells you where to look next.

guidance.title: You can take a moment
guidance.text: If this topic brings up some discomfort, that is all right. You do not have to decide what is in anyone's heart. Stay with the practice case. What does the form ask of people, and whose experience might be missing? You can think about this privately. The next step is to examine the process, without jumping to a conclusion about its cause.
